source: Kalayci, Raman, Dughmi (2025) Optimal Stopping vs Best-of-N for Inference Time Optimization
finding: Treats each LLM generation as opening a costly box in Weitzman's Pandora's Box problem. A UCB-style rule learns the stopping threshold without knowing the reward distribution. Rewards are rescaled across prompts with a Bradley-Terry style transform.
numbers: Same reward as non-adaptive Best-of-N with 15-35% fewer generations on average. At target acceptance 0.75 and above, savings rise from 15% to 35% as the target gets stricter.
quote: Viewing each generation as opening a costly "box" with random reward
limits: Quality is judged by reward models, not by correctness. Only 100 AlpacaFarm and 100 HH-RLHF prompts. Open-ended chat tasks, not math.
agent_relevance: Direct template for the S6 stop rule on sampling attempts: stop when the best-so-far beats a learned per-prompt threshold, not after a fixed N (G11, G12).

source: Kalayci, Raman, Dughmi (2025) Optimal Stopping vs Best-of-N, experiments section
finding: Large test grid. Adaptive stopping beats the best fixed N at equal average compute, but only modestly. Gains are largest when cost per sample is low or budgets are high.
numbers: 1,600 generation profiles (2 datasets x 100 prompts x 4 LLMs x 2 reward models), 960 responses each, 100 random orderings. Models: Gemma-2 9B, Llama-3.1 8B, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, Qwen-2.5 7B. Win rate over equal-budget Best-of-N above 54% across most cost settings, about 50% at minimal budget.
limits: A 54% win rate is a small edge. Cost per sample is a free parameter the designer must set. Authors flag tree search and model routing as untested.
agent_relevance: Expect a small, not large, gain from adaptive stopping on sampling alone. The main saving is compute, not quality.

source: Ehab, El Gadarri, Farias, Jozefiak, Moallemi (2026) OS-Pruner: Pruning Chains-of-Thought via Optimal Stopping
finding: Casts chain-of-thought pruning as optimal stopping. After each reasoning step a small learned module decides stop or continue by weighing expected accuracy gain against token cost. Plug-in, no retraining of the base model.
numbers: 20-60% shorter reasoning at under 2% accuracy loss on most model-dataset pairs. Tested on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, GPT-OSS-20B and DRPO-7B; GSM8K, MATH-500, AIME. Baselines: answer convergence, FlashThink, classification probe, all at thresholds 0.7 to 0.9.
quote: formulates chain-of-thought pruning as an optimal stopping problem
limits: Needs training of the stopping module per model. Preprint. Best results on easy and medium sets.
agent_relevance: Closest published match to S6 as an explicit value-of-continuing rule. Shows a stop rule beats fixed-threshold early exit on the accuracy-length frontier.

source: Ehab et al. (2026) OS-Pruner, per-dataset results
finding: Savings depend on difficulty. The stop rule cuts a lot on easy items and little on hard ones, as an optimal rule should.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B: length -59.3% on GSM8K (accuracy -0.7 points), -52.8% on MATH-500 (accuracy +2.7 points), only -6.9% on AIME at the best-AES point.
limits: Accuracy gain on MATH-500 may be partly overthinking removal. One model shown for these figures.
agent_relevance: Supports G11 and G12: spend little on easy items, keep budget on hard ones. A difficulty-sensitive stop rule does this by itself.

source: Ehab et al. (2026) OS-Pruner, baseline comparison table
finding: Fixed-threshold early-exit baselines lose accuracy fast when pushed for big savings. In one model block, answer-convergence at its most aggressive setting cuts 50.9% of GSM8K tokens but accuracy drops from 88.7 to 82.6.
numbers: Same block: FlashThink 64.5% saving with 82.5 accuracy; OS-Pruner 49.6% saving with 88.3 accuracy on GSM8K. Full-length baseline 88.7 accuracy, 1219 tokens.
limits: The model of that table block was not labelled in the extracted text. Authors built the comparison.
agent_relevance: Shows the cost of a naive stop rule: premature stops. A stop rule must price a wrong early stop, not only token cost.

source: Wang, Wang, Chen, Zeng, Wei, Li (2025) OptPO: Optimal Rollout Allocation for Test-time Policy Optimization
finding: Uses a Bayesian sequential probability ratio test (Wald-style) on majority votes: stop sampling when the posterior for the consensus answer passes a set error level (alpha = beta = 0.05). Kept rollouts feed PPO or GRPO updates.
numbers: Token savings roughly 15-60% vs fixed N=16 or 32 TTRL baselines at similar accuracy. Example GPQA with TTRL+PPO: tokens 262M to 144M, 45% saving. Over 40% savings on GPQA. Benchmarks: AIME 2024, AMC, MATH-500, GPQA; Qwen2.5 and Llama backbones.
quote: formulating the voting process as a Bayesian sequential probability ratio test
limits: Training-time use, not a single-query agent loop. Savings vary widely by cell (about 1% to 78%). Code not yet released at time of text.
agent_relevance: Gives a sound stop rule for the 2-4 independent attempts in S3: stop when an SPRT says the vote is decided.

source: Manzoor, Ascarza, Netzer (2025) Learning When to Quit in Sales Conversations
finding: Formalises quitting a sales call as optimal stopping. A GPT-4.1 stopping agent is fine-tuned by imitation of a retrospectively inferred optimal stopping policy. Works on raw text states.
numbers: 11,627 outbound sales calls from a European telecom firm. Cuts time on failed calls by 54% while keeping nearly all sales; reallocating the saved time raises expected sales by up to 37%. Quitting at 1 minute could have saved 55 hours.
quote: formalize the dynamic screening decision as an optimal stopping problem
limits: One firm, one language (Spanish), one campaign. Optimal policy is inferred after the fact, so it is an estimate.
agent_relevance: Shows an LLM can learn a stop policy over free text, and that hindsight-optimal labels are a usable training signal. Relevant to how S6 triggers might be learned.

source: Manzoor et al. (2025) Learning When to Quit, benchmarks and human comparison
finding: On the same GPT-4.1, a stopping agent trained on sequential reward beats one-shot classifiers (fine-tuned at 30, 60, 90 seconds), a sequential classifier ensemble, a deadline rule, and a deep-RL optimal stopping baseline (OSPG on embeddings). Human salespeople overweight a few salient cues of disinterest and mispredict failure risk.
numbers: Stopping agent with T=3 decision points beat all of these per the paper's figures 6a and 6b. Fine-tuning made the result insensitive to prompt wording. Failure could be predicted fairly well from the first 60 seconds.
limits: Exact margins per baseline were not recorded here. Human findings are about sales staff, not a lab stopping task.
agent_relevance: A good predictor is not a good stop rule: the rule must include time cost and forward value. Humans stop on salient cues, a bias not to copy.

source: Di Gioia (2026) Cognitive Friction: Decision-Theoretic Bounded Deliberation in Tool-Using Agents
finding: Triadic Cognitive Architecture prices each tool query and stops by an HJB-style boundary on belief and congestion. Tested in two simulated worlds. Names three agent failures: too much tool use, endless deliberation, averaging contradictory evidence.
numbers: TCA beats greedy ReAct by 36 viability points (medical grid, EMDG) and 33 integrity points (network triage, NSTG). Stopping rules alone recover at most 4 viability points. At step 0 ReAct picks the same slow tool in 100% of seeds; TCA picks the fast tool in 100%.
quote: stopping rules alone recover at most 4 viability points
limits: Simulations built by the author; one author; preprint. The headline gain comes from tool choice, not stopping.
agent_relevance: Warns that a stop rule alone gives little; choosing what to query next carries most of the gain. Fits our split between S6 stop rule and operator choice.

source: Di Gioia (2026) Cognitive Friction, real-LLM instantiation (appendix D)
finding: With GPT-4.1 on a made-up corpus (zero memorisation), the controller uses fewer retrieval calls but loses accuracy against always retrieving.
numbers: N=60 questions. AlwaysRetrieve: utility +5.33, exact match 0.817, 1.00 calls. TCA: utility +2.20, exact match 0.500, 0.63 calls, acts on 72% and defers on 28%. NeverRetrieve: exact match 0.000.
limits: Small N, one model. TCA scored lower utility than always-retrieve here, so the stop rule did not pay in this test.
agent_relevance: An honest negative: a decision-theoretic stop rule with weak value estimates can underperform a simple always-do-it policy. Calibrate costs before trusting.

source: Shaikh (2026) Knowing When to Ask for Help: Bayesian Self-Escalation in Hierarchical LLM Agents
finding: Frames hand-off from a small model to a strong one during generation as optimal stopping on a posterior of eventual success. Proves a time-varying threshold is optimal and that regret is controlled by calibration of the posterior. States plainly that the stopping math is not new.
numbers: Regret over the oracle is O(sqrt(L_t log K /(nT))) with n calibration trajectories of length T. Simulation: Bayesian optimal-stopping policy 96.0% accuracy at cost 0.111 escalating on 40% of queries; fixed rule 91.0%; always escalate 90.1%. Accuracy falls from 95.2% to 85.7% as calibration data is contaminated 0% to 30%.
quote: better calibration matters more than a smarter router
limits: Simulation uses a known generating process. The real-model test used a constant threshold, so it did not exercise the dynamic program (author's own note).
agent_relevance: For S6: calibration of the 'am I stuck' signal matters more than the cleverness of the rule. Matches the weak self-reported stuck signal (r = .17).

source: Shaikh (2026) Self-Escalation, first real-model execution (Qwen2.5-Coder 1.5B to 7B)
finding: In a real small-to-large code cascade, escalating during generation beats judging after the answer is complete. Two of three pre-registered predictions held.
numbers: Junior solves 62.3% of tasks, senior 80.9%. Senior rescues 54 of 97 junior failures (55.7%); 43 are failed by both. To reach 75% accuracy streaming uses 30.2% less compute (14,841 vs 21,273 tokens). At threshold 0.5 it escalates 37% of tasks at a mean 29% of the way through generation, for 74.7% accuracy.
limits: One model pair, one code benchmark. Shared-failure floor: some failures cannot be rescued. Version 1.1 preprint by one independent author.
agent_relevance: A mid-generation stop signal carries information (discrimination rises across generation) and can save about 30% compute.

source: Aggarwal, Madaan, Yang, Mausam (2023) Let's Sample Step by Step: Adaptive-Consistency
finding: Replaces fixed-N self-consistency with a stopping rule: sample until a Beta or Dirichlet model says the majority answer will hold with confidence 0.95. A sequential test, close to optimal stopping.
numbers: 17 reasoning and code datasets, 3 LLMs. Sample budget cut by up to 7.9x with average accuracy drop under 0.1%. Average cut by model: 4.4x GPT-3.5-Turbo, 1.9x Vicuna-13B, 3.4x Code-Davinci-002. Varying threshold 0.5 to 1 traded accuracy for cost smoothly; samples rise steeply near 1 while accuracy plateaus.
quote: reduces sample budget by up to 7.9 times with an average accuracy drop of less than 0.1%
limits: Older models (2023). Needs answers that can be compared for equality. Gains depend on how often the model agrees with itself.
agent_relevance: The simplest sound S3 stop rule: draw independent attempts until agreement is statistically settled. Direct support for G11.

source: Li, Yuan et al. (2024) Escape Sky-High Cost: Early-Stopping Self-Consistency (ICLR 2024)
finding: Splits sampling into small windows (size 5 in the example) and stops when all answers in one window agree. A control scheme picks window size and cap for a wanted cost-accuracy balance.
numbers: Sample count reduced by MATH -33.8%, GSM8K -80.1%, StrategyQA -76.8%, CommonsenseQA -78.5%, Coin Flip -84.2%, Last Letters -67.4% with comparable accuracy.
quote: Stop sampling when answers within a window are all the same
limits: Savings are smallest on the hardest set (MATH), where agreement comes late. Window rule is heuristic, argued by a Bernoulli bound.
agent_relevance: Shows the saving shrinks as difficulty rises, as the optimal stopping view predicts.

source: Liu and Wang (2025) Answer Convergence as a Signal for Early Stopping in Reasoning
finding: Models usually reach their final answer well before the chain of thought ends. Three stop methods: answer consistency, boosting the end-of-think token, and a supervised probe on internal activations.
numbers: On math tasks models converge after about 60% of reasoning steps. Five benchmarks, five open models. Answer consistency cuts tokens over 40% on NaturalQuestions while accuracy rises slightly. Learn-to-Stop: QwQ-32B GSM8K tokens 755.1 to 418.9 (-44%) for a 0.2% accuracy drop; GPQA -39.2%; NQ -46.2% (R1-Qwen-7B), -47.7% (R1-Qwen-32B), -46.4% (R1-Llama-70B) vs 34.1% for the 8B.
quote: models typically converge to their final answers after 60% of the reasoning steps
limits: Shallow signals like output consistency get unstable on hard tasks (MATH-500, GPQA); the supervised probe is more robust. Bigger models converge more confidently so gain more.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for G11: large share of reasoning tokens is waste on easy items. Also that output-only stop signals fail on hard items.

source: Mao, Yin, Zhu, Fang (2026) Early Stopping Chain-of-thoughts in LLMs (ES-CoT)
finding: At each 'wait' marker the model is asked for its current answer; a long run of identical step answers means convergence, so stop. Works on black-box models.
numbers: Tokens reduced by 16.08% on average with accuracy comparable to standard CoT. Six datasets, three LLMs.
limits: Smaller saving than white-box probes (c15, c19). Needs extra answer-probe calls. Compared with Dynasor and DEER, which probe similarly.
agent_relevance: A stop rule that works through the API alone, with no hidden states: usable in a scaffold.

source: Lee, Han, Kim (2026) Calibration-Free Early Stopping for CoT via E-processes
finding: Replaces threshold calibration with anytime-valid sequential tests (e-processes, Ville's inequality). Two streams, commit and abstain, run on one per-chunk signal. The false-alarm bound holds at every stopping time with no held-out data.
numbers: Qwen3 models, benchmarks incl. AIME and MATH-500, 12 model-dataset cells, 40 random splits. Matches or beats calibration-based Conformal Thinking on the token-accuracy frontier with zero calibration data; baselines used 50 validation items. Full-budget accuracy 0.726 in the shared table.
quote: Ville's inequality yields an anytime-valid signal-level false-alarm bound
limits: Guarantee is on signal-level false alarm, not on final-answer error. At small budgets some cells have no valid operating point.
agent_relevance: A stop rule that keeps its guarantee when the task shifts; useful because our agent cannot calibrate per task.

source: Min, Vaccarino et al. (2026) Stop When Reasoning Converges: PUMA
finding: Answer-level stop signals (confidence, trial-answer consistency) fire too soon. PUMA adds a detector for repeated, redundant reasoning steps and verifies before exiting.
numbers: 26.2% average token cut with accuracy kept, five reasoning models, five benchmarks. Counterfactual: of wrong early exits by confidence-based rules, 45.2% on average would have been right with full reasoning; for consistency-based rules 53.5%.
limits: Compared against DEER, Dynasor, CCoT. The premature-exit analysis and the retained-chain quality judge are the authors' own.
agent_relevance: Key risk for S6: about half of wrong early stops destroy a later self-correction. A stop rule needs a verify step before ending thinking.

source: Akgul, Kalayci, Kannan, Neiswanger, Prasanna (2025) LYNX: Learning Dynamic Exits for Confidence-Controlled Reasoning
finding: A hidden-state probe at natural cue tokens ('hmm', 'wait'), trained on forced exits, wrapped in split conformal prediction to control the rate of premature exits. One probe trained on math transfers to other tasks.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1-1.5B, QwQ-32B, Llama-3.1-Nemotron-8B. GSM8K: tokens down 40-65% with equal or better accuracy. MATH-500: up to +12 accuracy points with 35-60% fewer tokens. AIME 2024: baseline accuracy kept with over 50% token savings. CommonsenseQA zero-shot: up to 70% fewer tokens.
quote: continuing to reason long after they internally have enough information to answer correctly
limits: Needs open-weight hidden states. Conformal guarantee holds only if calibration data match deployment.
agent_relevance: Stopping can raise accuracy, not only save tokens, because overthinking hurts. Supports G11.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Making Small Language Models Efficient Reasoners
finding: After supervised fine-tuning, small distilled models fail to find a good stopping point and produce long, repetitive output. Fixes: temperature scaling on the end-of-sequence probability, and a length-penalised RL method (TLDR).
numbers: TLDR cuts token use by about 50% with minimal to no accuracy loss versus the SFT baseline. Four benchmarks: MATH500, AMC, AIME24, OlympiadBench. Temperature scaling beat s1 budget forcing.
quote: the post-SFT model fails to determine the optimal stopping point of the reasoning process
limits: Small models only. Wrong responses are more verbose than right ones, so length is itself a failure signal.
agent_relevance: A long answer is a cue to stop or restart, a code-readable trigger for S6.

source: Belloni, Chen, Wei (2026) Online Pandora's Box for Contextual LLM Cascading
finding: Models querying a sequence of LLM APIs as a contextual Pandora's Box. Learns Weitzman reservation indices by GMM with UCB bounds; proves sublinear regret when reward is seen only for the deployed output.
numbers: Simulated regimes. Oracle queries 1.30-1.78 boxes per period on average, so one-shot bandits that query one model lose option value. A FrugalGPT-style fixed cascade is clearly worse when the best order varies with context. Known vs unknown-reward variants differ by at most about 0.17% of oracle utility.
limits: Simulation and synthetic environments; the formal guarantees do not strictly cover the experiments (authors say so).
agent_relevance: Supports having code, not the model, pick the next attempt or tool by an index and stop when the best seen exceeds the index of the rest.

source: Qian (2026) Auditing LLM Program Search for Bermudan Stopping with Primal-Dual Certificates
finding: LLM agents wrote Python exercise policies for Bermudan options, a classical optimal stopping problem with a duality certificate. None beat the standard Ridge Longstaff-Schwartz baseline beyond Monte Carlo noise.
numbers: 24 generation attempts, two pipelines, a six-pair feedback ablation, a frozen holdout. Holdout gap scores within 0.002 of Ridge. On six 1-D puts, 99% of the estimated gap is dual-bound looseness. Structured memory gave no benefit over score-only memory.
quote: No selected generated program improves on Ridge LSMC consistently
limits: Small search scale; the dual bound could not certify progress at that scale. One task family.
agent_relevance: A warning: LLM search over stop policies did not improve a known strong stopping method. Do not expect the model to invent a better rule than the textbook one.

source: Hiremath and Hiremath (2026) Calibration Drift Under Reasoning
finding: Claims more reasoning budget can make a model overconfident. Proposes a CABStop rule to stop before calibration worsens.
numbers: Llama-3.1-8B calibration error (ECE) by budget: 0.044 (none), 0.104 (light), 0.050 (medium), 0.015 (heavy), not the predicted U-shape. 1,368 API calls but only 574 valid trap responses (42%). Llama-3.3-70B tested only without reasoning, so inconclusive.
limits: Weak evidence: the 8B result does not match their own theory, selection bias from the 42% validity rate, one model family. Treat as unproven.
agent_relevance: Boundary case. Do not cite as established that longer thinking worsens calibration.

source: Koh, Choi, Kwon, Baek, Kim (2026) </think> Doesn't Stop Reasoning: Spurious CoT Termination
finding: Forcing an end-of-think token at an early exit point often does not stop reasoning. The model keeps reasoning in the answer phase and emits another end token.
numbers: Regeneration rate above 20% for QwQ-32B and above 15% for R1-Distill-14B; below 3% for R1-Distill-1.5B and Qwen3-14B. Four models, five benchmarks, two early-exit methods (DEER, DynaSoR). Example: 1,090 reasoning plus 760 answer tokens vs 2,116 plus 371 for full CoT. Attention biasing toward the injected token reduces it.
limits: Describes how early exit is implemented, not a failure of the stop decision itself.
agent_relevance: Our stop must be enforced by code and the answer phase checked; a model told to stop may keep going.

source: Fang et al. (2026) LLM-OSDA: Optimal-Stopping Dynamic Auction for Native Advertising
finding: Chooses the turn at which to insert one ad in a chat by Bellman optimisation, with a learned StopNet trained on recorded dialogues.
numbers: On simulated conversations, revenue proxy rises 2.51% over first-turn insertion and 12.00% over final-turn insertion with the same dialogue model.
limits: Simulated users and proxy revenue. Not about reasoning.
agent_relevance: Another example of a Bellman stop rule over turns of an LLM dialogue; little transfer to reasoning.

source: Wang (2026) Uncertainty-Aware Sequential Decision Rules for Event-Triggered LLM Invocation
finding: Treats when to call an expensive LLM as a risk-based stopping problem; unifies event-triggered, SPRT, CUSUM and Bayesian triggers; proves threshold optimality and sublinear regret.
numbers: On turbofan degradation data with real LLM calls: sublinear regret (below 1 for principled triggers); 92.9% of 1,600 LLM diagnoses reach grounding score 0.75; anomaly-score risk functions beat alternatives by about an order of magnitude on Pareto area. Six baselines incl. a RouteLLM-style router and contextual bandits.
limits: Only abstract and opening text were read. Domain is sensor streams.
agent_relevance: Calls to a heavy tool can be gated by a cheap stop-style trigger.

source: Search result: arXiv listings for 'secretary problem' with LLMs (this session)
finding: Searches of arXiv abstracts found no study giving the classic secretary problem (1/e rule) to language models and comparing them with people. The only language-model hit was a 2026 proof of the strong secretary conjecture for linear matroids written with an AI model. Others are learning-augmented secretary theory.
numbers: Hits: 2609.20797 (AI-assisted proof), 2601.07482, 2411.09854, 2410.06583, 2409.20460 (secretary with predictions). Title search for 'secretary problem' plus language models returned zero results.
limits: Arxiv listings only; web search quota was spent and OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and the arXiv API returned rate-limit errors. Non-arXiv venues were not covered, so the gap may be a coverage gap.
agent_relevance: Do not claim anything about LLM behaviour on the secretary task. Report as an unfilled gap.

source: Search result: arXiv listings for 'optimal stopping' with LLMs (this session)
finding: Explicit optimal-stopping language in LLM papers is recent (2025-2026) and mostly engineering. The earlier line (2023-24) uses sequential tests without the name.
limits: Only listing titles seen for 2608.13404, 2606.21906, 2606.20591, 2604.19795; not opened.
agent_relevance: The field converges on one design: sequential test or index rule plus a verify step, not human-style heuristics.
